deeperExplanation.question: What if I cannot tell whether the tool helped?
deeperExplanation.answer: Unclear is an acceptable result. You may need a simpler comparison, another setting or more time. You can also decide the experiment is not relevant to your current goal. Write what you do know, including whether the task itself became crowded. A useful experiment does not always end in a clear improvement. It helps you make a more informed choice about what to explore next.

sections.narration:
Welcome. Today we are exploring Experiment Without Grading Yourself. You try a tool once and immediately ask whether you did it correctly. The practice becomes another performance, and the interesting details disappear behind a pass or fail.

In this session, we will choose an experiment question, observe one change, and leave an uncertain result open. I will explain the idea, show a visual example, and invite you to try it in a small experience of your own. You can ask me a question or switch to reading at any point. We will finish by choosing what, if anything, you want to take into a real conversation.

The result can be helpful, neutral, uncomfortable or unclear. Each gives information about how to proceed. You are not the result of the experiment.

You try a tool once and immediately ask whether you did it correctly. The practice becomes another performance, and the interesting details disappear behind a pass or fail.

When you change several things at once, it becomes difficult to understand the experience. Choose one small difference such as a little more space before answering or one meaning chunk at a time. Compare similar prompts. Keep the observation about effort, connection, willingness or communication rather than turning the recording into a total score.

A changed, unchanged or uncertain experience is information, not a grade. You do not have to report relief for this attempt to count as exploration.

sections.narration: Run one small comparison in private practice. Save the question, observation and next choice in three lines. During focused practice, you can deliberately explore this one tool. In an everyday conversation, give most of your attention to the message and the other person. A familiar support can be available if it helps; you do not have to monitor the tool throughout the exchange.
